citation.title: Research Note: A More Powerful Test Statistic for Reasoning about Interference between Units

standing_assumptions:
The work is a nine-page research note (Political Analysis (2016) 24:395–403; printed page = PDF page + 394, so printed p. 395 is PDF p. 1). It states no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof. Its mathematics is the randomization-test procedure of Section 1, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov formula of footnote 3, the three numbered displays (1)–(3) and the unnumbered application model of Section 3; everything else is simulation and one application. Everything quoted below was read from the page images (the staged 110-dpi images, and 200- and 400-dpi renderings of the staged PDF for subscripts and footnotes).
(S1) Outcomes under interference. p. 395 (PDF p. 1), Section 1: “In a randomized experiment with $n = 4$ subjects connected via a fixed network, the response of subject $i = 1$ might depend on the different ways that treatment is assigned to the whole network. When the treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z}$, provides treatment to persons 2 and 3, $\mathbf{z} = \{0, 1, 1, 0\}$, person $i = 1$ might respond one way, $y_{i=1,\mathbf{z}=\{0,1,1,0\}}$, and when treatment is assigned to persons 3 and 4, $\mathbf{z} = \{0, 0, 1, 1\}$ person $i = 1$ might act another way, $y_{i=1,\mathbf{z}=\{0,0,1,1\}}$. More generally, we might say that if the experiment had a causal effect on person $i$, then her outcome would differ under different realizations of the experimental treatment as a whole $y_{i,\mathbf{z}} \neq y_{i,\mathbf{z}'}$.” Footnote 1 (p. 395): “In simpler settings, where treatment given to one individual has no effect on any other individual, we tend to write $y_{i,Z_i=1} \neq y_{i,Z_i=0}$ to say that treatment had a causal effect on person $i$.”
(S2) The testing procedure. p. 396 (PDF p. 2), Section 1: “Say $Y_i$ is the observed outcome, and we hypothesize that units do not interfere and also that $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$. We can assess which (if any) hypothesized values of $\tau$ appear implausible from the perspective of the data by: (1) mapping the hypothesis about unobserved quantities to observed data using the identity $Y_i = Z_i y_{i,Z_i=1} + (1 - Z_i) y_{i,Z_i=0}$—noticing that if $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$ then $y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau$ (by substituting from the hypothesized relationship into the observed data identity); (2) using this result to adjust the observed outcome to represent what would be implied by the hypothesis for a given $\tau_0$ such that $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau_0$; and (3) under the hypothesis, $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ should have no systematic relationship with treatment assignment, so we can summarize this relationship with a test statistic, $\mathcal{T}(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}, Z_i)$. A distribution of values for this test statistic arises from repetitions of the treatment assignment process (new draws of $\mathbf{z}$ from all of the ways that such treatment assignment vectors could have been produced); and finally (4) a $p$ value arises by comparing the observed test statistic, $\mathcal{T}(Y_i, Z_i)$ against the distribution of that test statistic that characterizes the hypothesis.” The paper gives no formula for the $p$ value and does not say which tail (or tails) of the reference distribution is used.
(S3) The KS statistic. Footnote 3, p. 396 (PDF p. 2): “If the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) of the treated units is $F_1$ and the ECDF of the control units is $F_0$, then the KS test statistic is $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{KS}} = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\left[F_1(y_{i,0}) - F_0(y_{i,0})\right]$, where $F(x) = (1/n)\sum_{i=1}^{n} I(x_i \le x)$ records the proportion of the distribution of $x$ at or below $x_i$ (Hollander 1999, section 5.4).”
(S4) Validity as the paper states it. p. 397 (PDF p. 3): “Such results mean that a test of the sharp null of no effects based on a known randomization using any effect increasing test statistic ought to be a valid test (in that the test should produce $p$ values less than $\alpha$ no more than $100\alpha\%$ of the time when the null is true) even though different test statistics may imply different power against false hypotheses.”
(S5) The simple SSR statistic and the no-interference simulation. p. 397 (PDF p. 3), Section 2: “For example, the implication of the constant, additive effects model, $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau$, only changes the distribution of outcomes for units in the treated condition.” Equation (1), with the sentence that introduces it: “The simplest version of the sum-of-squared-residual (SSR) test statistic merely sums the difference between the mean of the outcome implied by the hypothesis and individual outcomes, thereby including the correlation between treated and control outcomes as a part of the distribution of the statistic: $$\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i \left(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} - \bar{\tilde y}_{i,Z_i=0}\right)^2 \quad (1)$$” Design: “we created a small simulation study of 256 units with half assigned to a binary treatment completely at random. We compared the performance of the two test statistics on two outcomes with no interference—a Normal outcome and a skewed outcome, both with mean of 10 and standard deviation of 1, as shown in Fig. 1.” Models: “We compared two models of effects—a constant additive effects model in which $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$ and a constant multiplicative effects model in which $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} \cdot \tau$. We set the truth to be the sharp null of no effects such that the true $\tau = 0$ for the additive model and the true $\tau = 1$ for the multiplicative model.”
(S6) The SSR statistic with network information. p. 399 (PDF p. 5), Section 2.1: “In the case where we know the fixed binary adjacency matrix of a social network, $\mathbf{S}$, where a given entry in the $n \times n$ matrix is 1 if two units are adjacent and 0 if two units are not adjacent, and where we imagine that network attributes (like degree) of a node play a role in the mechanism by which treatment propagates, the idea of assessing model fit rather than closeness of distributions leads naturally to the SSRs from a least squares regression of $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ on $Z_i$ and $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$ (i.e., the number of directly connected nodes assigned treatment) as well as the $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ (i.e., the degree of the node). If we collected $Z_i$, $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$, and $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ into a matrix $\mathbf{X}$, and fit the $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ as a linear function of $\mathbf{X}$ with fitted coefficients $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ then we could define the test statistic as $$\mathcal{T}(y_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i \left(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\right)^2. \quad (2)$$” (In display (2) the first argument is printed as an italic $y_0$; in display (1) and in footnote 3 it is a bold $\mathbf{y}_0$.)
(S7) The network model, design and tests. p. 399 (PDF p. 5), Section 2.2: “Their model of treatment propagation was $$\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{w}, \beta, \tau) = \frac{\beta + (1 - w_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{S})}{\beta + (1 - z_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S})}\,\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}. \quad (3)$$ Briefly, this model posits that treatment effects can depend on either direct assignment to treatment ($\mathbf{z}$) governed by $\beta$ or spillover as an increasing (but flattening) function of the number of directly connected treated neighbors ($\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$) and is governed by $\tau$. So, we have a model with two parameters. The network used by BFP involves 256 nodes connected in an undirected, random graph with node degree ranging from 0 to 10 (mean degree 4, 95% of nodes with degree between 1 and 8, five unconnected nodes with degree 0). Treatment is assigned to 50% of the nodes completely at random in the BFP example.” pp. 399–400 (PDF pp. 5–6): “We assess three versions of the SSR test statistic versus three versions of the KS test statistic. The first, described above, we call the SSR + Design test statistic because it represents information about how treatment is assigned to the nodes, $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$. The second version of the SSR test statistic (SSR + Degree) only includes network degree, $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$, and excludes information about the treatment status of other nodes. And the third version (SSR) includes only treatment assignment $\mathbf{z}$.” p. 400: “For each test statistic, we tested the hypothesis $\tau = \tau_0, \beta = \tau_0$ by using a simulated permutation test: we sampled 1000 permutations. We executed that test 10,000 times for each pair of parameters. The proportion of $p$ values from that test less than .05 is plotted in Fig. 3: darker values show fewer rejections, lighter values record more rejections.” p. 400: “The KS + Design and KS + Degree panels show the power of applying the KS test to residuals from linear models including network degree only (the + Degree version) or degree and also the number of treated neighbors (the +Design version).” Fig. 3 caption, p. 401 (PDF p. 7): “Proportion of $p$ values less than .05 for tests of joint hypotheses about $\tau$ and $\beta$ for the model in equation (3). Darker values mean rare rejection. White means rejection always. Truth is shown at the intersection of the straight lines $\tau = .5, \beta = 2$. Each panel shows a different test statistic. The SSR tests refer to equation (2), the KS tests refer to the expression in footnote 3.”
(S8) The application model. p. 400 (PDF p. 6), Section 3: “Coppock reanalyzes the experimental results with an eye toward spillover, constructing a social network based on similarity on W-NOMINATE ideology scores. Coppock hypothesized that ideologically similar legislators would be more likely to share information.” “With distance matrix $\Gamma$, Coppock evaluated the model: $$\mathbf{y}_0 = \mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}} - \beta_1\mathbf{z} - \beta_2 g(\Gamma\mathbf{z}),$$ where $g$ is a function that normalizes the sums of distances to treated neighbors to have unit variance. This model has a direct effect ($\beta_1$) and an indirect effect ($\beta_2$) that is linear in the distances to treated neighbors. Coppock evaluated this spillover model using the SSR + Design statistic as presented in this article.”
(S9) Conventions of this list (not the paper's notation). In the targets, $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ (or $a$) is the vector of hypothesis-adjusted outcomes $u_i = \tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$, held fixed while the assignment is redrawn; $z \in \{0,1\}^n$ is an assignment with $n_g = \#\{i : z_i = g\}$ units in group $g$ ($g = 1$ treated, $g = 0$ control); $\bar u_g$ or $m_g$ is the mean of $u$ over group $g$; $R(u,z) = \sum_i (u_i - \bar u_{z_i})^2$ is the residual sum of squares from the least-squares regression of $u$ on an intercept and $z$ (the statistic that the paper calls ‘SSR’, as the released code computes it); $F_g(t) = n_g^{-1}\#\{i : z_i = g,\ u_i \le t\}$ and $D(u,z) = \max_i |F_1(u_i) - F_0(u_i)|$ is the two-sided KS distance (as the released code computes it). The expressions $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ in displays (2) and (3) are read componentwise: for unit $i$, $(z^TS)_i = \sum_j z_j S_{ji}$ (the number of treated neighbours) and $(1^TS)_i = \sum_j S_{ji}$ (the degree). A randomization design is a probability distribution on a finite set $\Omega \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ of assignments; ‘completely at random’ with half treated is read as the uniform distribution on the assignments with exactly $n/2$ treated units. Witnesses and corrected statements are the validators' and Sol's constructions unless a passage is marked as printed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, the two sentences after the quotation of BFP's advice, as repaired by Sol: the effect increasing property stated, and sharp-null validity for any test statistic
canonical_claim.location: p. 397 (PDF p. 3), first paragraph, second and third sentences
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P016-E005, smallest_repair), verbatim: “Replace the two explanatory sentences after the quotation with: A statistic is effect increasing if, at a fixed treatment assignment, raising treated responses and lowering control responses cannot decrease it. The quoted advice about distributional divergence does not imply this directional condition. Under a sharp null, calibrating any specified statistic under the known assignment law gives a valid test; unbiasedness against alternatives is a separate question.”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (the validator's derivation.md, sections 2–3).
(EI) A statistic $T : \mathbb{R}^n \times \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is effect increasing if for every $z$ and all $y, y' \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $y'_i \ge y_i$ whenever $z_i = 1$ and $y'_i \le y_i$ whenever $z_i = 0$, $T(y',z) \ge T(y,z)$.
(i) The difference in group means $T(y,z) = \bar y_{z=1} - \bar y_{z=0}$ (defined for $z$ with both groups non-empty) satisfies (EI).
(ii) The two-sided KS distance $D$ does not satisfy (EI), and neither does the signed maximum printed in footnote 3 (witness P016-T11 (i)): being small for similar and large for divergent distributions does not imply (EI).
(iii) [Sharp-null validity needs no property of the statistic] Let $\Omega$ be a finite set of assignments, $q$ a probability distribution on $\Omega$ with $q(z) > 0$ for all $z \in \Omega$, and $Z \sim q$. Let $s : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be any function (under the sharp null of no effects the outcome vector $y^0$ is the same under every assignment, and $s(z) = T(y^0, z)$ for an arbitrary statistic $T$). Define $$p_U(z) = \sum_{w \in \Omega : s(w) \ge s(z)} q(w), \qquad p_L(z) = \sum_{w \in \Omega : s(w) \le s(z)} q(w), \qquad p_2(z) = \min\{1, 2\min(p_U(z), p_L(z))\}.$$ Then for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$: $\Pr\{p_U(Z) \le \alpha\} \le \alpha$, $\Pr\{p_L(Z) \le \alpha\} \le \alpha$ and $\Pr\{p_2(Z) \le \alpha\} \le \alpha$. In particular each test produces “$p$ values less than $\alpha$ no more than $100\alpha\%$ of the time when the null is true”, whatever the statistic.
(iv) [Check on the smallest example] For $y^0 = (0,1,2,3)$, complete randomization of two of four units and $s = D(y^0,\cdot)$: $s = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 1$ and $p_U = \tfrac13, 1, 1, 1, 1, \tfrac13$ on the treated sets $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{2,4\},\{3,4\}$, so $\Pr\{p_U(Z) \le \alpha\}$ is $0$ for $\alpha < \tfrac13$, $\tfrac13$ for $\tfrac13 \le \alpha < 1$ and $1$ for $\alpha = 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [As printed: p. 397 (PDF p. 3)] “Rosenbaum (2002, Proposition 4 and 5, section 2.9) presents results proving that test statistics with this property (“effect increasing” test statistics) produce an unbiased test of the hypothesis of no effects or positive effects when the positive effects involve one parameter. Such results mean that a test of the sharp null of no effects based on a known randomization using any effect increasing test statistic ought to be a valid test (in that the test should produce $p$ values less than $\alpha$ no more than $100\alpha\%$ of the time when the null is true) even though different test statistics may imply different power against false hypotheses.” [Sharp null and known randomization: p. 396 (PDF p. 2), steps (1)–(4)] standing assumption (S2). The paper prints no $p$-value formula; $p_U$ and $p_L$ are the exact inclusive upper- and lower-tail probabilities under the assignment distribution, and $p_2$ is the two-sided rule of the released simulation code computed with exact tail probabilities.

Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair; prior_correction.status ‘correct’); repair cost: none, a correction to explanatory prose. (EI) and (i)–(ii) are section 2 of the validator's derivation.md; (iii) is its section 3 (the proof orders the distinct score values, accumulates their probabilities and uses a union bound for $p_2$); (iv) is the table at the end of that section. (iii) is also the result that P016-T8 (b) and P016-T21 invoke.

canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witnesses (the validator's; not in the paper) that a simulated randomization test which (1) forms each tail as the raw count of the $B$ sampled reference statistics at or beyond the observed statistic, without counting the observed statistic itself, (2) takes $p_{\mathrm{raw}} = \min\{1, 2\min(L,U)/B\}$ with $L = \#\{b : T_b \le T_0\}$ and $U = \#\{b : T_b \ge T_0\}$, and (3) rejects when $p_{\mathrm{raw}} \le \alpha$, can reject a true sharp hypothesis with probability greater than $\alpha$. Rule (1)–(3) is that of the archived simulation code; the rule printed in the paper is rejection when $p < .05$, which these witnesses do not refute (P016-T14 (b)).
(i) [No ties] Let $T_0, T_1, \ldots, T_B$ be exchangeable real random variables that are almost surely pairwise distinct ($T_0$ the observed statistic). Then $K = \#\{b : T_b < T_0\}$ is uniform on $\{0, \ldots, B\}$, $L = K$, $U = B - K$, and with $c = \lfloor \alpha B/2 \rfloor$ and $2c < B$: $$\Pr\{p_{\mathrm{raw}} \le \alpha\} = \frac{2(c+1)}{B+1}.$$ For $\alpha = \tfrac1{20}$ this is $\tfrac{52}{1001} = \tfrac4{77} > \tfrac1{20}$ at $B = 1000$ and $\tfrac{502}{10001} > \tfrac1{20}$ at $B = 10000$.
(ii) [A finite randomization design, with ties] Sixteen units $i = 0, \ldots, 15$; all $\binom{16}{8} = 12870$ assignments with exactly eight treated units equally likely; the sharp null of no effect holds with outcomes $y_i = 2^i$; the statistic is the residual sum of squares on an intercept and $z$, which for treated set $A$ with $s = \sum_{i \in A} 2^i$, $S = 65535$ and $Q = \sum_i 4^i = 1431655765$ equals $R = Q - \{s^2 + (S - s)^2\}/8$. It takes exactly $M = 6435$ distinct values, each on exactly two assignments (a treated set and its complement). The observed assignment $Z_0$ and the reference assignments $Z_1, \ldots, Z_B$ are independent draws from the design, and $T_b = R(y, Z_b)$. Then for $\alpha = \tfrac1{20}$ and $c = B/40$ the null rejection probability of rule (1)–(3) is $$S_B(c) = \frac{2}{M}\sum_{r=1}^{M}\sum_{k=0}^{c}\binom{B}{k}\left(\frac{r}{M}\right)^{k}\left(\frac{M-r}{M}\right)^{B-k},$$ and $S_{1000}(25) = 0.051792651792\ldots > \tfrac1{20}$ and $S_{10000}(250) = 0.050039580346\ldots > \tfrac1{20}$. Moreover $$\frac{2(c+1)}{B+1} - \frac{2}{M} \le S_B(c) \le \frac{2(c+1)}{B+1},$$ and for $B = 1000$, $c = 25$ the lower bound is $\tfrac{4}{77} - \tfrac{2}{6435} = \tfrac{2326}{45045} > \tfrac1{20}$. With rejection when $p_{\mathrm{raw}} < \tfrac1{20}$ instead (cutoffs $c = 24$ and $c = 249$) the rejection probabilities are $S_{1000}(24) = 0.049794649794\ldots$ and $S_{10000}(249) = 0.049839600344\ldots$, both below $\tfrac1{20}$.
(iii) [A raw $p$ value of zero] In (ii), $\Pr\{p_{\mathrm{raw}} = 0\} = S_B(0) = 2\sum_{r=1}^{M-1}(M - r)^B / M^{B+1} > 0$ (for $B = 1000$ it is $0.001846625\ldots$).

canonical_claim.note: P016-E008 is rated an error, Minor, and is a defect of the archived code, not a false printed statement (Sol: false_as_printed false; the printed strict rule has level at most .05 with fresh exchangeable reference draws). It is a target because the finding rests on an exact formal counterexample and its repair changes a formula (the Monte Carlo $p$ value); priority 3. Sol's verdict: confirmed_in_part (upheld on re-run), evidence type exact_counterexample. Not established, and not asserted here: that the paper's own 256-unit tests exceeded .05, that the reported rates of about 4% and 2% are wrong, or anything about the application's fixed assignment bank. (i) is the ‘continuous-rank’ calculation of section 2 of the validator's derivation.md (it has an atomless premise that a finite design does not satisfy, and is recorded as the mechanism); (ii) and (iii) are section 3, the validator's finite-assignment counterexample, with the exact reduced fractions in exact_probabilities.json in the same folder. For this list the enumeration ($M = 6435$, multiplicity 2), $S_{1000}(25)$, $S_{1000}(24)$, $S_{1000}(0)$ and the lower bound were recomputed with exact rational arithmetic; the two values at $B = 10000$ are the validator's and were not recomputed. A formalizer can prove the violation at $B = 1000$ from the lower bound (the validator proves the bounds by comparing the sum with $\int_0^1 \Pr\{\mathrm{Bin}(B,q) \le c\}\,dq = (c+1)/(B+1)$); the lower bound at $B = 10000$, $\tfrac{502}{10001} - \tfrac{2}{6435}$, is below $\tfrac1{20}$, so the violation at $B = 10000$ needs the exact sum.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The level of the simulated permutation tests of Section 2.2, as repaired by Sol: the printed strict cutoff, and the rank-corrected Monte Carlo $p$ value
canonical_claim.location: p. 400 (PDF p. 6), Section 2.2, first and second paragraphs; p. 397 (PDF p. 3), the parenthesis on validity
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P016-E008, smallest_repair), verbatim: “For the simulation's fixed .05 cutoff at B=1000 or B=10000, change the code's <= ALPHA to < ALPHA, matching the printed rule. For valid finite-reference p-values at arbitrary thresholds, replace each empirical tail count C/B by (1+C)/(B+1) and retain the capped doubled minimum for a two-sided test. State the exchangeability premise and distinguish the empirical size report from any claim about the archived weak-cutoff algorithm. Page 397's theoretical exact-randomization statement needs no repair. The application's bank-dependent construction needs a separate justification before certifying the rank correction there.”
Sol's corrected text (prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim: “The exact randomization-law validity statement is correct. At alpha=.05, the printed p<.05 rule is conservative with B=1000 or B=10000 fresh exchangeable reference draws. The archived simulations instead use p<=.05 with raw empirical tails, which does not in general control size at .05. For a fixed statistic whose observed and B reference values are exchangeable under the true null, use p_U=(1+sum_b 1{T_b>=T_obs})/(B+1), and reverse the inequality for p_L. Then min(1,2 min(p_U,p_L)) is valid. Fixed-bank sampling and bank-dependent exposure construction require a separate exchangeability justification. This correction alone does not refute or revise the reported empirical rejection frequencies.”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (the validator's derivation.md, sections 2 and 4). Let $B \ge 1$ and let $T_0, T_1, \ldots, T_B$ be real random variables whose joint distribution is exchangeable (invariant under every permutation of the $B + 1$ indices); ties are allowed. $T_0$ is the observed statistic and $T_1, \ldots, T_B$ the reference statistics. Put $L = \#\{b \ge 1 : T_b \le T_0\}$, $U = \#\{b \ge 1 : T_b \ge T_0\}$ and $p_{\mathrm{raw}} = \min\{1, 2\min(L,U)/B\}$.
(a) [Rank bound] For every integer $c$ with $0 \le c \le B$: $\Pr\{L \le c\} \le \dfrac{c+1}{B+1}$ and $\Pr\{U \le c\} \le \dfrac{c+1}{B+1}$.
(b) [The printed strict rule at the printed level] For every $\alpha \in (0,1)$: $\Pr\{p_{\mathrm{raw}} < \alpha\} \le \dfrac{2\lceil \alpha B/2 \rceil}{B+1}$. For $\alpha = \tfrac1{20}$ this bound is $\tfrac{50}{1001} < \tfrac1{20}$ at $B = 1000$ and $\tfrac{500}{10001} < \tfrac1{20}$ at $B = 10000$.
(c) [Rank-corrected $p$ values] Put $p_L^+ = \dfrac{1+L}{B+1}$, $p_U^+ = \dfrac{1+U}{B+1}$ and $p_2^+ = \min\{1, 2\min(p_L^+, p_U^+)\}$. Then for every $a \in [0,1]$: $\Pr\{p_L^+ \le a\} \le \dfrac{\lfloor a(B+1) \rfloor}{B+1} \le a$ and likewise for $p_U^+$; and $\Pr\{p_2^+ \le \alpha\} \le \alpha$ for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$.
(d) [When the hypothesis of exchangeability holds] If $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is fixed (the uniformity outcomes under a true sharp hypothesis), $Z_0, Z_1, \ldots, Z_B$ are independent draws from the same assignment distribution and $T_b = T(y, Z_b)$ for one fixed function $T$, then $(T_0, \ldots, T_B)$ is exchangeable.
(e) [Exact tails need no correction] With the exact assignment distribution in place of sampled reference draws, the inclusive tail probabilities and their capped doubled minimum are valid at every level: P016-T12 (iii).

Repair the calibration objective so that it summarizes affected units rather than taking the median over 128 unchanged controls and 128 treated units.”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (the validator's derivation.md, sections 2, 4 and 7). Let $N = 2m$ units with $z \in \{0,1\}^N$ having exactly $m$ treated units, $y \in \mathbb{R}^N$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}$. Put $d_i(a) = |y_i(1 + z_i(a-1)) - (y_i + z_it)|$, and let $\mathrm{med}$ denote the average of the $m$-th and $(m+1)$-th smallest of $N$ values.
(a) $d_i(a) = 0$ for every control unit and $d_i(a) = |(a-1)y_i - t|$ for every treated unit.
(b) [The criterion sees one treated unit] $\mathrm{med}\{d_1(a), \ldots, d_N(a)\} = \tfrac12\min_{i : z_i = 1}|(a-1)y_i - t|$.
(c) For every treated unit $j$ with $y_j \ne 0$, the value $a_j = 1 + t/y_j$ makes the criterion $0$, its global minimum; at $a_j$ every other treated unit has $d_i(a_j) = |t|\,|y_i/y_j - 1|$, which is non-zero when $t \ne 0$ and $y_i \ne y_j$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 396] “Say $Y_i$ is the observed outcome, and we hypothesize that units do not interfere and also that $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$. We can assess which (if any) hypothesized values of $\tau$ appear implausible from the perspective of the data by: (1) mapping the hypothesis about unobserved quantities to observed data using the identity $Y_i = Z_i y_{i,Z_i=1} + (1 - Z_i) y_{i,Z_i=0}$—noticing that if $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$ then $y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau$ (by substituting from the hypothesized relationship into the observed data identity); (2) using this result to adjust the observed outcome to represent what would be implied by the hypothesis for a given $\tau_0$ such that $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau_0$”.
[Printed, p. 399] “Their model of treatment propagation was $$\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{w}, \beta, \tau) = \frac{\beta + (1 - w_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{S})}{\beta + (1 - z_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S})}\,\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}. \quad (3)$$”
Formal reading. (a) [The printed identity] For real numbers $y_{i,Z_i=0}$, $y_{i,Z_i=1}$, $\tau$ and $Z_i \in \{0,1\}$: if $Y_i = Z_i y_{i,Z_i=1} + (1 - Z_i) y_{i,Z_i=0}$ and $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$, then $y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau$. Consequently, if the hypothesis is true with $\tau = \tau_0$, the adjusted outcome $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau_0$ equals $y_{i,Z_i=0}$ whatever the assignment.
(b) [The same mapping for equation (3); the properties are not printed] Let $S$ be an $n \times n$ real matrix with non-negative entries (the adjacency matrix), $\beta > 0$ and $\tau \in \mathbb{R}$, and for $v \in \{0,1\}^n$ put $c_i(v) = \beta + (1 - v_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2 (v^TS)_i)$ with $(v^TS)_i = \sum_j v_jS_{ji}$. Read componentwise, equation (3) is $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{w}, \beta, \tau)_i = \dfrac{c_i(w)}{c_i(z)}\,y_{\mathbf{z},i}$. Then: (b1) $c_i(v) > 0$ for all $v$ and $i$, so the ratio is defined; (b2) $c_i(\mathbf{0}) = 1$ for every $i$, so the outcome in the uniformity trial (no unit treated) implied by the model is $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{0}, \beta, \tau)_i = y_{\mathbf{z},i}/c_i(z)$; (b3) $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{z}, \beta, \tau) = \mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}$, and for assignments $z, w, w'$, applying the map from $w$ to $w'$ to $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{w}, \beta, \tau)$ gives $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{w}', \beta, \tau)$; (b4) if the outcomes under every assignment follow the model with parameters $(\beta, \tau)$, that is $y_{\mathbf{z},i} = c_i(z)\,y_{\mathbf{0},i}$ for all $z$ and $i$, then the adjusted outcome $y_{\mathbf{z},i}/c_i(z)$ computed with those parameters equals $y_{\mathbf{0},i}$ for every assignment $z$: under the true hypothesis the adjusted outcome vector does not depend on the assignment.

[Model (3): p. 399 (PDF p. 5)] “this model posits that treatment effects can depend on either direct assignment to treatment ($\mathbf{z}$) governed by $\beta$ or spillover as an increasing (but flattening) function of the number of directly connected treated neighbors ($\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$) and is governed by $\tau$”; $\mathbf{S}$ is “the fixed binary adjacency matrix of a social network ... where a given entry in the $n \times n$ matrix is 1 if two units are adjacent and 0 if two units are not adjacent”. The paper does not state what $\mathcal{H}$ returns; it is read, with BFP and the released code, as the vector of outcomes under assignment $\mathbf{w}$ implied by the outcomes $\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}$ under assignment $\mathbf{z}$, and the display is read componentwise (the scalar $w_i$ and the vector $\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{S}$ appear side by side in it). [The condition with no unit treated: p. 397 (PDF p. 3)] for the BFP model the adjusted outcome is written $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0,Z_{-i}=0}$, “where $Z_{-i} = 0$ means “when all units other than $i$ are also not treated””. canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P016-H2 (sharp hypotheses about treatment propagation are assessed by mapping observed outcomes to the uniformity trial implied by the hypothesis and comparing a statistic with its distribution under the known design) is a description of a method; its mathematical content is the adjustment identity, which the paper prints for the additive model, and the corresponding property of model (3), which the paper uses and does not state. (a) is an exact finite-sample identity, hence priority 3; (b) is this list's formal reading of what the readers checked (candidates.json, held_up: equation (3) with $w = 0$ gives the adjustment in simulation/models.R and agrees with the coded forward and inverse maps to within $3 \times 10^{-14}$). The second half of the claim, the comparison with the randomization distribution, is P016-T12 (iii) (exact tails) and P016-T14 (sampled reference draws), and its application to the simulation of Section 2.2 is P016-T21. Findings P016-E001 and P016-N002 (both Minor) concern step (4) of the same paragraph and a sentence of Section 2, not the identity; their corrected statements are P016-T8 and P016-T17. There is no validator artifact for this target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.2: ‘All of these test statistics are valid—they reject the true null of $\tau = .5, \beta = 2$ no more than 5% of the time at $\alpha = .05$’, repeated as ‘all of the tests are valid in the sense of rejecting the truth no more than 5% of the time when $\alpha = .05$’
canonical_claim.location: p. 400 (PDF p. 6), Section 2.2, first and second paragraphs; Fig. 3 and its caption, p. 401 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 400, first paragraph] “For each test statistic, we tested the hypothesis $\tau = \tau_0, \beta = \tau_0$ by using a simulated permutation test: we sampled 1000 permutations. We executed that test 10,000 times for each pair of parameters. The proportion of $p$ values from that test less than .05 is plotted in Fig. 3: darker values show fewer rejections, lighter values record more rejections. All of these test statistics are valid—they reject the true null of $\tau = .5, \beta = 2$ no more than 5% of the time at $\alpha = .05$—and the plots are darkest in the area where the two lines showing the true parameters intersect.”
[Printed, p. 400, second paragraph] “Again, all of the tests are valid in the sense of rejecting the truth no more than 5% of the time when $\alpha = .05$ although all of these tests are conservative: the SSR-based tests rejected the truth roughly 4% of the 10,000 simulations but the KS tests rejected the truth roughly 2% of the time.”
Formal reading of the validity statement (the level bound; the reported rates of about 4% and 2% are simulation results and are not part of the target). Setting of Section 2.2: $n = 256$ units, a fixed symmetric binary adjacency matrix $S$, and the design that treats exactly 128 units, all such assignments equally likely. The outcomes follow model (3) with the true parameters $(\beta, \tau) = (2, \tfrac12)$: $y_{\mathbf{z},i} = c_i(z)\,y_{\mathbf{0},i}$ with $c_i(z) = \beta + (1 - z_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2 (z^TS)_i)$. A test statistic is any function $T(u, z)$ of the adjusted outcome vector $u$, the assignment $z$ and the fixed $S$; the six statistics of the paper are of this form (the residual sum of squares of $u$ on an intercept, $z$, $z^TS$ and $1^TS$; on an intercept, $z$ and $1^TS$; on an intercept and $z$; and the KS distance between the treated and control groups of the residuals of $u$ on an intercept, $z^TS$ and $1^TS$; of the residuals on an intercept and $1^TS$; and of $u$ itself). Testing the true hypothesis means computing $u_i = Y_i/c_i(Z)$ from the observed outcomes $Y = y_{\mathbf{Z}}$ with the true parameters. Claims, for every such $T$:
(i) $u = y_{\mathbf{0}}$ for every realized assignment $Z$ (P016-T20 (b4)).
(ii) [Exact reference distribution] With the exact inclusive upper-tail probability $p_U$, lower-tail probability $p_L$, or their capped doubled minimum $p_2$, computed from the assignment distribution and the statistic $z \mapsto T(u, z)$: $\Pr\{p \le .05\} \le .05$, and hence $\Pr\{p < .05\} \le .05$ (P016-T12 (iii)).
(iii) [Simulated reference distribution, as described in the text] If the observed assignment $Z_0$ and $B = 1000$ sampled reference assignments $Z_1, \ldots, Z_B$ are independent draws from the design, $T_b = T(u, Z_b)$, and $p_{\mathrm{raw}} = \min\{1, 2\min(L,U)/B\}$ with $L = \#\{b \ge 1 : T_b \le T_0\}$ and $U = \#\{b \ge 1 : T_b \ge T_0\}$, then the test that rejects when $p_{\mathrm{raw}} < .05$ rejects the true hypothesis with probability at most $\tfrac{50}{1001} < .05$; with $B = 10000$ the bound is $\tfrac{500}{10001} < .05$ (P016-T14 (b), (d)).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Model (3) and the network: p. 399 (PDF p. 5)] standing assumption (S7); “Treatment is assigned to 50% of the nodes completely at random in the BFP example”; the network is “undirected”. [The six statistics: pp. 399–400 (PDF pp. 5–6)] “SSR + Design”, “SSR + Degree”, “SSR” (equation (2) with the regressors named in the text; an intercept is included, finding P016-E002), and the KS statistic of footnote 3 applied to “residuals from linear models including network degree only (the + Degree version) or degree and also the number of treated neighbors (the +Design version)” or with no adjustment. [Hypothesis tested] the text prints “$\tau = \tau_0, \beta = \tau_0$”; the joint hypothesis $\tau = \tau_0$, $\beta = \beta_0$ is meant (finding P016-E011, P016-T16 (c)), and the true null is $\tau = .5$, $\beta = 2$. [The test] “a simulated permutation test: we sampled 1000 permutations”; “$p$ values ... less than .05”. The paper prints no $p$-value formula and no tail; the released code uses $p_{\mathrm{raw}}$ (P016-T13).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P016-H4 has a mathematical part, the level bound, and an empirical part, that the tests are conservative with null rejection rates of about 4% (SSR) and 2% (KS); only the bound is a target. It is an exact finite-sample statement, hence priority 3. It is a corollary of three targets on this list and is stated separately because it is the note's one explicit claim of a guarantee: (i) is P016-T20 (b4), (ii) is P016-T12 (iii), (iii) is P016-T14 (b) with (d). The claim holds for every statistic, so the six statistics need not be formalized one by one. Finding P016-E008 (Minor) concerns this claim: the archived simulation code rejects when $p_{\mathrm{raw}} \le .05$, for which the bound fails in general (P016-T13), while the printed rule $p < .05$ satisfies it, so the printed statement stands; Sol records false_as_printed false. Findings P016-E006 and P016-E009 also touch the passage (the unstated tail rule; 10,000 experiments of 1000 permutations in the text against the reverse in the archived defaults) and do not change the bound, which is given for both values of $B$. Whether the published Fig. 3 was produced with the strict or the weak cutoff cannot be determined from the staged material.
